notes.trap: `reduce(...)` is an alias of `aggregate(...)` added in 3.4.0, and it has no NULL skipping. A single NULL element turns `acc + x` into NULL, and the result stays NULL from then on. This differs from `sum(...)`, which ignores NULLs.
notes.example_sql: SELECT reduce(array(1, NULL, 3), 0, (acc, x) -> acc + x)

notes.trap: Without a comparator, NULL elements go to the END of the array, whereas ascending `sort_array(...)` puts them first. With a comparator, NULLs are not handled for you: the lambda must deal with them, because a comparator that returns NULL raises an error.

`exists(...)` uses three-valued logic. If no element satisfies the predicate and the predicate evaluates to NULL for some element, the result is NULL, not false, so a WHERE clause silently drops the row.
The optional second lambda argument is a 0-based index, unlike the 1-based `element_at(...)` and `slice(...)`. Elements for which the predicate returns NULL are dropped, just like false.
notes.example_sql: SELECT CAST(filter(array(10, 20, 30), (x, i) -> i = 1) AS STRING)

notes.trap: If no element makes the predicate false and the predicate evaluates to NULL for some element, `forall(...)` returns NULL rather than true. It only returns false when at least one element definitely fails.

The result has the union of keys from both maps, and a key missing from one map is passed to the lambda with NULL as its value. A plain `v1 + v2` or `concat(...)` therefore yields NULL for those keys unless you wrap the values in `coalesce(...)`.
notes.example_sql: SELECT element_at(map_zip_with(map('a', 1), map('b', 2), (k, v1, v2) -> v1 + v2), 'a')

notes.trap: The optional second lambda argument is a 0-based position, not 1-based as in `element_at(...)`, so code ported from 1-based logic will be off by one.
notes.example_sql: SELECT CAST(transform(array(10, 20, 30), (x, i) -> i) AS STRING)
